definition: A Special Purpose Acquisition Company (SPAC) is a publicly traded shell company, most often incorporated in the state of Delaware, that enables taking a private company public through a reverse merger. The SPAC is established by a sponsor who raises money through an initial public offering (IPO). IPO units are typically sold for $10 each and include a share of stock and a fraction of a warrant (or, in some cases, a warrant to purchase part of a share). The funds raised are placed in a trust account to benefit public stockholders, who have the right to redeem their shares after a merger target is identified. This redemption feature provides IPO investors with a fixed return. The sponsor, often structured as a limited liability company, manages the SPAC. In exchange, the sponsor receives a “promotion,” which is generally 20% of the SPAC’s equity after the IPO, issued as “founder shares” for a nominal price. special needs / Special Purpose Acquisition Company (SPAC) Dictionary compilation | 26 September 2026 Additionally, the sponsor invests alongside the IPO to cover underwriting fees and other expenses, as trust funds cannot be used for these costs. When the SPAC merges with a private company (a process known as de-SPACing), it may also raise new funds through a private investment in public equity (PIPE). SPAC charters set a deadline, normally 18 to 24 months, to complete a merger with a private company. If the SPAC fails to do so, it must liquidate, returning the funds in the trust (including any interest) to public stockholders. In such cases, the sponsor’s founder shares become worthless. See e.g., Delman v. GigAcquisitions3, LLC, 288 A.3d 692, 701 (Del. Ch. 2023). For more information, see: Types of Registered Offerings [Written in December of 2024 by the Cornell Law School Securities Law Clinic]
